newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Troubled Mir's navigation devices fixed - expert.
newsitem.headline: Troubled Mir's navigation devices fixed - expert.

text.p: The latest navigation problem of the crippled Mir space station has been fixed and the devices that keep its solar panels lined up to the Sun to gain maximum power are now working, a mission control expert said on Sunday.
"Yesterday evening all 12 gyrodines have been put into motion and they now work in a stable manner," the expert, who declined to be named, told Reuters by telephone.
The specialist did not say how the devices had been repaired and who -- mission control by remote commands or the three-men Russian-U.S. crew carried out the repair works.

Deputy mission chief Sergei Krikalyov said on Thursday there had been an unexplained malfunction in all of the station's gyrodines. The result was that the cosmonauts were having to fire their rocket engines to keep Mir lined up to the Sun and prevent a further loss of electric power.
The station lost up to half its power on June 25 after a collision with an unmanned cargo craft punctured the Spektr scientific module and cut off supplies from some panels.

A cargo craft is on the way to Mir with relief supplies and is expected to dock with the ageing station on Monday. The expert said the cosmonauts were resting on Sunday to accumulate energy for the docking.
Commander Vasily Tsibliyev and engineer Alexander Lazutkin of Russia and British-born U.S. astronaut Michael Foale were all feeling fine, he said.

The expert also said the Progress cargo craft, launched on Saturday from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan which Russia leases, has coped with a problem it had encountered when it took off -- a panel of a solar battery did not unfold properly.
"It unfolded fully today and the ship is getting 100 percent energy," he said. "All systems of the Progress work normally."
The supplies aboard the unmanned Progress M-35 include oxygen, food and water as well as repair tools.
The fixing of the gyrodines should come as a relief for the crew after the latest bout of trouble which was disclosed on Saturday but took place six days ago.
Russian and NASA officials confirmed on Saturday that there had been a mystery leak from the holed Spektr module.

A Russian specialist said: "Five days ago, in one of our communications with the crew, we were told they had seen flakes and bubbles from an unknown source leaking from the Spektr module." He added it was not fuel.
The leak had been into space rather than inside, and there had been no repeat since that single incident.
